title: Throughput benchmarking harness and methodology (loadgen configs, repeatability, warmup) - WIP
content:
Status: WIP - collecting more runs across A100/RTX6000 + quantized profiles and validating tooling reproducibility.

Purpose
- Capture our recommended harness and measurement methodology for throughput experiments. This is the canonical how-to for perf investigations: load generator configs, warmup best-practices, variance controls, and quick checks for common bottlenecks.

Goals
- Report tokens/sec and sustained qps under realistic request distributions.
- Make runs repeatable across hosts and between engineers.
- Separate model/hardware/compiler noise from workload characteristics.
- Surface common regressions (batching regressions, kernel fallback, memory thrash).

High-level approach
1) Fix as many moving parts as possible: model version, compilation artifacts, docker image, kernel selection policy.
2) Warmup the runtime to steady state (KV cache + JIT/compiles).
3) Run multiple independent trials with identical configs; report median and p90 of tokens/sec and p99 latency.
4) Collect system-level and GPU counters concurrently (nvidia-smi, DCGM, perf counters).
5) Run microbenchmarks (single-request latency) + steady-state throughput tests.

Environment pinning (must-do for repeatability)
- Docker image: use full digest (e.g., quay.io/redwood/serving:2026-01-12@sha256:...) not :latest.
- Model artifact: model repo commit hash / model sha and compilation artifact id. e.g., redwood-v1-fp16@sha256:abcd1234.
- Hardware: record GPU model, driver version, CUDA/cuDNN versions, kernel.
- Kernel selection: for experiments we prefer to freeze kernel/func selection when comparing changes. Use env REDWOOD_KERNEL_LOCK=1 when reproducing.
- CPU governor: set to performance (sudo cpupower frequency-set -g performance) to avoid CPU frequency variability.
- Isolate host: run on minimally loaded instance; use cgroups or dedicated node when possible.
- NUMA: pin process to appropriate NUMA nodes (taskset / numactl) when benchmarking multi-socket hosts.

Load generator configuration (recommended fields)
- Duration: 10m steady-state after warmup (longer for low-variance).
- Warmup: 2m – 5m depending on workoad (see warmup section).
- Concurrency: choose ranges around expected operating point: e.g., [4,8,16,32] for small models; higher for batching-friendly models.
- Batch size: explicit control (0 == dynamic batching), test static batch sizes and dynamic.
- Sequence length distribution: use realistic histogram or explicit percentiles (p50/p90/p99).
- Request size seeds: use fixed RNG seed for payload generation (seed=42).
- Request arrival pattern: Poisson (recommended) to mimic real traffic; also test constant QPS for saturation curves.
- Inter-request variability: model name, temperature, stop tokens influence token production; keep fixed when measuring throughput.

Example loadgen command (CLI)
- rli-loadgen --model redwood-v1-fp16 --image-digest sha256:abcd --duration 600 --warmup 120 --concurrency 16 --batch-size 8 --seq-hist p50:128,p90:512,p99:1024 --arrival poisson --seed 42 --metrics-endpoint http://localhost:9090/metrics

Warmup best-practices (why and how)
- Why: warmup brings the runtime to steady state by populating KV caches, triggering any lazy JIT/compiles, and letting batch timers stabilize. Without warmup, the first N minutes can show artificially low throughput or high latency.
- KV cache: for autoregressive models, supply prefix tokens in warmup that match the typical prompt length distribution so the KV cache size matches steady-state.
- JIT/compiles: run a short canonical request set that covers typical sequence lengths and tensor shapes to force kernel selection/compilation before measurements.
- Quantized paths: run warmups on the same quantization profile to ensure any one-time quantization initialization happens ahead of measurement.
- Checklist:
  - Run 2–5 minutes of warmup traffic with same seq distribution.
  - Run an explicit compile-warmup: 10 single-shot long-seq runs to force kernels.
  - Ensure memory growth has stabilized (check docker stats/gpu memory).
  - Confirm no kernel fallback events in logs (grep kernel-fallback).

Repeatability and statistical rigor
- Trials: run N >= 5 independent trials, spaced out (e.g., 10 minutes apart) to avoid thermal coupling when necessary.
- Report: median tokens/sec, inter-trial standard deviation, min, max. Also report p50/p95/p99 request latency during steady-state window.
- Randomization: keep seeds fixed across trials for request payloads; vary only the trial number.
- Stability checks: compute coefficients of variation (std/mean). If > 5–8% for tokens/sec, increase run length or investigate noise sources.

What to collect (minimum)
- Application metrics: tokens/sec, requests/sec, avg/p50/p95/p99 latency, batch size distribution, batch latency breakdown (queue + compute + post).
- GPU: utilization, memory allocation, SM/compute % (DCGM), GPU power, encoder/decoder occupancy.
- Host: CPU usage (user/sys/idle), interrupts, context switches, iowait, network tx/rx.
- OS: dmesg for OOMs/driver messages.
- Runtime logs: kernel selection events, fallback warnings, compilation durations.
- Build metadata: docker image digest, model artifact id, commit hashes for runtime and loadgen.

Common failure modes and quick triage
- Low tokens/sec & low GPU util: likely batching misconfiguration (small concurrency or disabled batching) or excessive host CPU throttling. Check batch size distribution and cpu wait.
- High latency p99 spikes: look for rare large batches causing queueing, or occasional kernel fallback/compiles. Inspect runtime logs for compile events.
- Throughput regressions after code change: confirm kernel lock and compilation artifacts identical; rerun with REDWOOD_KERNEL_LOCK=1; if still regressed, collect perf + nvprof to compare instruction mixes.
- Memory thrash / OOM: check memory growth during warmup; if growth continues in steady-state, there may be a leak or non-evicted KV cache entries.

Microbenchmarks to isolate bottlenecks
- Single-request cold latency (no KV) to measure end-to-end baseline.
- Single-request warm (with KV) to measure decoder token latency.
- Batched synthetic payloads with controlled seq len to isolate kernel performance.
- Throughput at increasing concurrency to find knee point (concurrency sweep).

Example reporting template (CSV columns)
- run_id, host, gpu_model, driver, runtime_commit, model_artifact, duration_s, warmup_s, concurrency, batch_size, seq_p50, seq_p90, tokens_per_sec, reqs_per_sec, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, gpu_util_pct, notes

Next actions (todo)
- Add automated job in perf CI to run the canonical scenario nightly on an isolated A100 and record baseline. (owner: Liam)
- Capture more quantized-profile runs (int8/ggml) to see kernel selection variance (owner: Chen).
- Integrate DCGM exporter to our Prometheus scrape and add dashboard for tokens/sec vs GPU metrics (owner: Marta).

Notes and open questions
- How much warmup is needed for real customer traffic (varies by prompt distribution). We should instrument a few large customers to characterize warmup patterns.
- Parking compile artifacts between runs vs always forcing a recompile: for release checks we should test both.

References
- See linked artifacts above for previous methodology drafts and the harness repo PRs.

(End of doc - add run outputs and full logs in the same folder once we have the next set of runs.)
